The department has also admitted that it does maintain a Bell nine-passenger helicopter at Victoria and its crew has not received search and rescue training either. subsubtopic: DEMAND FOR RESIGNATIONS OF FOUR MINISTERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadians are moved with admiration, noting the respect shown to the time-honoured British tradition of ministerial responsibility which prompted the resignation of Lord Carrington, Foreign Secretary of the United Kingdom government. I therefore move, seconded by the member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay):
That this House demand that the Government of Canada return to this honourable tradition, so regrettably neglected by the arrogance demonstrated opposite, by requiring the resignations of the Minister of Finance for his high interest rates and for failure to honour his promise "Vote Liberal and the price of gasoline will stay down": of the Minister of Employment and Immigration for his failures demonstrated in more than one million unemployed; of the Prime Minister and the Solicitor General for their failure to protect the security service from unfair trial.
These resignations, and many more, will signal to Canadians and the world that responsible government has been returned to Canada.

THE CONSTITUTION
subsubtopic: PREFERENCE FOR CONSTITUTIONAL MONARCHY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my colleagues and I wish to voice the warmest words of welcome and best wishes to Her Majesty the Queen and Prince Philip on the occasion of their upcoming visit to Canada. Our constitutional monarchy symbolizes the epitome of democracy. The Queen is not the representative of the majority of the people but the people themselves.
I suppose an integral movement in any well executed pirouette would be an about-face. The Prime Minister has demonstrated in regard to the Queen that he is fast on his feet but slow in his reaction time to policies and principles-above all, principles. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen (Mr. King):
That this House affirm its recognition of the rich legacy bequeathed to us by the British parliamentary system of government, our preference for a constitutional monarchy along with the checks and balances which guarantee the primacy of the individual, his or her rights, privileges and basic freedoms, and that this House enhance this legacy building on-not chipping away at-the symbols and institutions, traditions and customs which have led us along the road to full nationhood.

IMPORT COMPENSATION PROGRAM-REASONS FOR MINISTER'S APPEAL TO REFINERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. The minister has known for at least six months that there is a serious problem with the manner in which the import compensation program is working. Common sense would dictate that the program should ensure maximum utilization of domestic crude oil, with the remaining requirements being made up with the cheapest possible offshore supplies. In this way, maximum benefit would accrue to governments in the form of taxes, industry in the form of cash flows, and consumers in the form of cheaper gasoline and heating oil. Instead of correcting this program, last Thursday the minister announced that he is asking eastern Canadian refiners to refrain from buying cheap offshore oil. Will the minister please explain to the House how this will benefit Canadian consumers which, after all, is the original reason behind the import compensation program?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: IMPORT COMPENSATION PROGRAM-REASONS FOR MINISTER'S APPEAL TO REFINERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would very simply explain to the hon. member that one should not ask companies to walk away from valid contracts which have been entered into. I asked the companies to act in whatever way they can without breaking contracts and endangering future medium and longterm security of supply for Canada.
As the hon. member well knows, part of that problem arose from the fact that the government of Alberta arbitrarily cut back production last year by 120,000 barrels a day. Some refiners had to enter contracts with foreign countries to make up for that loss. They have to honour those contracts until they expire. I have indicated to the refiners that once their contracts expire they should renegotiate those contracts bearing in mind the availability of Canadian crude and also ensuring medium and long-term supply for Canadians.
As far as the immediate steps which they can take are concerned, I have said that "when there is Canadian crude available", as there is, "do not go for spot market purchases at the expense of Canadian crude. If you are buying it on the spot market, buy it at the expense of your other foreign suppliers."

subtopic: IMPORT COMPENSATION PROGRAM-REASONS FOR MINISTER'S APPEAL TO REFINERS
speechtext: The minister knows that these long-term contracts were entered into at the instigation of the federal government and were resisted by the industry.

Having demonstrated the government's willingness to protect Petro-Canada's and Mexico's interest,
April 5, 1982

why is the government now reluctant to use its regulatory authority to protect the interests of domestic producers and also, incidentally, the interests of consumers who would be paying less for their gasoline and heating oil if they were using Canadian crude rather than the high cost imported crude which the companies were forced to contract for, by the government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):

subtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT REGULATORY AUTHORITY

Madam Speaker, the hon. member is not telling the truth when he says that the government has forced the refiners to enter into long-term contracts. The contracts entered into by the companies have been made on their own as commercial business decisions.
As far as the supply from the Government of Mexico is concerned, my hon. friend will recall that the Government of Canada entered into that contract with Mexico at a time when there were shortages in the world and everyone was scrambling for supplies. We succeeded in getting 50,000 barrels a day and we intend to honour that contract. With respect to policy steps which were announced last week, I must remind the hon. member that the Canadian Petroleum Association has come out in support of the steps we have taken.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a very serious question of privilege which involves my rights as a citizen and as a member of Parliament.
A letter was addressed to me as a member of Parliament; it was correctly addressed; there can be no mistake about the name and address of the intended recipient, myself. My mail was inspected by X-ray machine by the RCMP and then opened and read by someone in the Prime Minister's Office. The RCMP X-ray inspection date stamp "Safe to Handle" is dated March 29, 1982.

April 5, 1982
Privilege - Mr. Stew an
Then, apparently, the letter was sent to the Prime Minister's Office, where it was opened and read and initialled by "B.J.M." The date and time stamp from the Prime Minister's Office is "digits 000050 received PMO 10.25 a.m., March 30, 1982". Another set of numbers was stamped on the letter and then obliterated by a white opaqueing agent. The numbers are discernible from the reverse and are "2089 133."
I received the letter in my office by regular mail on Friday, April 2, 1982. I am wondering how many similar occasions there have been. Madam Speaker, I believe I have a bona fide question of privilege. I demand an explanation from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his ironclad assurance that his office does not routinely monitor mail for members of Parliament, such as this letter or any other members' letters, or letters from persons who are not partial to his philosophy, his actions or his deeds.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have some comments I should like to make in the House concerning this bill which, I feel, is extremely important. In fact, I feel that the draft legislation we are now discussing, Madam Speaker, has consequences that could be compared to those of the bill on constitutional reform. When the subject is fiscal arrangements, relations between the provinces and the federal government and sums of money that run into hundreds of billions of dollars, I think we can say, without exaggeration, that this legislation is of vital importance both to the entire country and to each province individually, and more specifically, where it concerns the federal government's contribution to health services and post-secondary education in the provinces. I have said, and I say it again without hesitation, that this bill is particularly important. A number of hon. members have spoken to the bill, Mr. Speaker. We are now at the third reading stage, and I assume that we are getting ready to pass this bill.
A number of widely differing views have been expressed, and as the provinces have also indicated earlier that they disagreed with the federal government, I therefore feel that today, as a member of this House, it is my duty to remind the government that it is important to negotiate and to spend a considerable amount of time negotiating, especially when large amounts of money are involved and objectives are being discussed that are vital to the entire Canadian nation. I know there have been all kinds of comments for months, and that the provinces were almost unanimous in opposing this bill. Of course, we had some amendments. At first, even the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) had some trouble with the figures he tabled in the House, some mistakes were made, there were some computation errors, and all this has been part of the debate. We are now about to adopt this legislation, and we are also faced with the fact that we have, in a sense, failed; that is, we would have preferred to give the provinces some proposals or a decision they would have been able to accept unanimously.
The members on the opposite side will say that the provinces have a voracious appetite, but they will have to admit that the
Federal Transfers to Provinces
government has made decisions without sufficient consultation with the provinces. And speaking of the provinces, my own province has, through its representatives, made a number of comments on this legislation, and I have also listened to my colleagues opposite as they explained the nature of the proposals contained in the bill, while quoting very specific figures. Although they are saying in Quebec that under this legislation, Quebec will see its payments reduced, it is a fact that in absolute terms, Quebec will be receiving several thousand dollars more than last year. On the other hand, there are those who say that if the federal government had not changed the formula, Quebec would be getting even more money in the next few years.
At least one thing is clear. With the new formula, the federal government will be getting a better deal than before and will be paying out $5 billion less over the next five years than it would be paying under the old formula. There are no two ways about it. And we know for a fact that the costs of the services in question which are vital to all Canadians are increasing and will continue to do so according to the economic scenario we have now. In those circumstances, obviously the provinces are not wildly enthusiastic, nor is my own province wildly enthusiastic about this reduction in funds, compared with projections made several years ago, and it is perfectly normal for the representatives of my province to express their disappointment with the decision or decisions made by the federal government, and their impact on Quebec particularly, as a result of the formula changeover.
Mr. Speaker, previous speakers have already mentioned quite a number of figures in their speeches, which I found quite interesting, but I have no intention of repeating them. I think we have had an ample supply of statistical data provided by all three parties and by a number of members of this House.
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is extremely important that the government should show more respect in its relations with the provinces. This legislation is essential because it involves billions of dollars and absolutely vital services, and the federal government should recognize its responsibility as the originator of these services and programs. It should also recognize and accept the fact that the provinces are entitled to not only make representations with respect to the allocation of the funds they need but also with respect to the economic situation facing us today.
The present government cannot ignore these circumstances and disclaim responsibility for the problems confronting Canadians today. The way I see it, the record of this government's administration during the past 15 years has not been particularly encouraging, which has probably led the provinces to claim that, deficit for deficit, the federal government has not been setting a particularly good example.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
The provincial governments, including the government in my own province, may be criticized, and they have been, for their present deficits. However, I feel that the worst example has been set by the present federal government, which has been increasing the national debt and its deficits during the last 15 years I have been here in the House.
However, one can only go so far, and it seems the government has realized this. In fact, the Minister of Finance has been dragging us through the mill during the past few months, and the provinces are, as it were, squirming in a financial strait-jacket, because the federal government is reducing its deficit by cutting funds to the provinces. At this point, I must say, and I have said it before, that there may be dangerous developments in the years to come. In other areas, there is the distinct impression that the government, because of its financial circumstances for which it is, in fact, to blame, is increasingly making decisions that go against the wishes of the provinces and are not preceded by the negotiations appropriate to a federal system.

speechtext:
I seem to be getting some comments from the other side of the House, Mr. Speaker. On the subject of federal-provincial relations, I feel that in a federal system that purports to respect the status of the provinces, there is at least an obligation to encourage negotiations and conduct them in a manner that reflects respect for the true federal concept. That is not what is happening.
I understand that a number of hon. members, and it has become more apparent in the last year or so, have fallen into the habit of blaming the provinces for situations that are prevalent across Canada. I feel that we who are sitting in this federal Parliament have an obligation to demand that this government should respect its partners, the provinces, without exception. Members opposite seem to think this is highly amusing. During the Constitution debate, there were some unfortunate incidents, thanks to the persistence and dedication of an opposition that earnestly wanted all the parties concerned, all governments in Canada, to participate in the exercise of constitutional reform, and I feel that we, in any case, need have no regrets for having made a special effort to make the government understand the spirit of federalism.
When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) states that, in his opinion, co-operative federalism is dead, we have to ask ourselves serious questions and the provinces have to be very concerned, as do all Canadians, about the nature of future negotiations. In other fields, Mr. Speaker, I could refer to certain comments which I also heard. It is obvious that this government has decided to reduce its negotiating process and its discussions with the provinces because it is tired of dealing and discussing with them, which is of course dangerous, because the people opposite will then try to convince us daily that we have to work for national unity. This same government
will try to take credit for saving the country and working in the interests of Canada. However, it is not by making unilateral decisions that we can promote and strengthen the bonds of real federalism. I believe that I am quite justified in reminding this government how important it is at every opportunity to allow the provinces to take part in a greater number of major national decisions and to find compromise solutions with the provinces, especially when dealing with such an important bill as the one which we are now discussing at the third reading stage. This bill deals with billions of dollars and has very important consequences for the service sectors involved. I fail to understand why the government has not managed to bring the provinces to an acceptable consensus and compromise. I must conclude that, because of its actions, attitude and arrogance, the government has succeeded in creating a climate of suspicion.
In every area, whether it be economic development, constitutional reform or fiscal arrangements, a climate of suspicion has been created in this Parliament because of the government's reprehensible and regrettable attitude. This is why the premiers and the ministers responsible cannot trust it at federal-provincial meetings. Of course, this multiplies the problems, and because of this, negotiations take longer. However, since this is somewhat annoying for the Prime Minister of Canada and his cabinet, they make an increasing number of decisions on their own, which is regrettable and goes against the very principles of true federalism which must survive because the future of the country is based on this concept. The present government no longer believes in it. I say once again that we shall see more and more direct action by the federal government about economic development and more and more programs governed, imposed and administered federally without proper consultation with the provinces. I sincerely regret this and I must warn the government that it is not the way to save the country or to serve it well.
I could refer to the history of the last fifteen years, especially in my province. I know that this will also shock my colleagues opposite. However, as I have said before, the record points to an embarrassing failure on economic matters and the Constitution on the part of a government which would now want us to believe that it has succeeded. If we talk about the economy, the situation in which we now find ourselves is hard to believe. As for this bill, I can appreciate the arguments of the various provinces and especially my own concerning provincial needs. I believe that we must go beyond party politics when we are dealing with such an essential piece of legislation.
I suggest that it is both possible and necessary to do so. I do not take hon. members opposite to task for having quoted exact figures in connection with the computation formula or the bill, nor do I question their figures; yet, they should agree with me that the old formula would have brought more money in and that the Quebec Minister of Finance is complaining

I think it is therefore important, Mr. Speaker, to remind hon. members that well-prepared negotiations are necessary when such major legislative measures are brought forward. I was about to say that the climate of trust which existed 15 years ago has vanished entirely. We have seen all sorts and we have had various indications for a while that the mistrust which has prevailed in this Parliament is clearly due to an arrogant attitude on the part of this government, and because of this mistrust, problems in Quebec become still more serious whenever the federal government is involved. I should like to take this opportunity to invite hon. members opposite to make an additional effort to encourage discussions and negotiations between the two governments. Both governments cannot continue to stir up a confrontation, because this would prove too costly for our constituents who do not deserve that partisanship be shown at their expense.
I think that the time has come to remind all my colleagues that negotiations and the respect of our provincial governments are essential, and I think that all those who still believe in a true federalism would agree, but should one believe in that true federalism? When I hear the responsible government authorities, the ministers of the Crown increasingly give the impression that they are determined to act alone without consulting the provinces, that is not the way to strengthen the ties among the regions and to ensure a promising future to the country, Mr. Speaker. The study of this legislation today affords me the opportunity to urge the government to reflect seriously on the negotiations with the provinces, which have greatly disintegrated and deteriorated in the past few years. However, the Leader of this Government in the opinion of

millions of Canadians, seemed capable of uniting this country, but over the past 15 years and at present, I do not think any government has managed better to tear our country apart and to create such dreadful conditions as those we are now experiencing. Under the circumstances, instead of turning away, of ruling out further negotiations and denying the proper respect which must be shown to provincial governments, it would be to the advantage of this government to resume negotiations more seriously than ever before and to urge governments to co-operate in promoting the economic recovery of the country.
Not long ago, the Right Hon. Prime Minister appealed to the unions, urging them to co-operate with the federal government, because otherwise he would once again be forced to make unilateral decisions. During the past 15 years, the Prime Minister has had plenty of time to bring the unions, businesses and the provinces to the negotiating table, but as a result of his unbending attitude, instead of bringing these people together, he has done the exact opposite. Today, the situation being what it is, we must make a last effort and urge the government to be far more attentive to the problems facing the provinces and to those confronting millions of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to dwell further on this bill, which, although I do understand its ramifications, is not easy to understand since it is a sophisticated piece of legislation. In any case, because of this bill, the provinces will once more be obliged to seek other funding sources if they wish to maintain the same level of health services and post-secondary education. To reduce its deficit and lighten its financial burden, the federal government has decided to shift some of this burden to the provinces. Considering the present economic situation, for which I hold the federal government largely responsible, there will be other opportunities to prove this.
I think this government would have been well-advised to listen to the suggestion made by my colleague, the member for Kingston and the Islands, who asked for a two-year extension during which time the government would have a chance to prove to the provinces that it has sufficient flexibility to make federalism more viable and more acceptable. It is true that in Quebec, people are becoming more and more disenchanted with federalism, which was certainly not the case a few years ago. However, during the past 15 years, Mr. Speaker, and I say it once again, we have seen Quebecers becoming increasingly alienated from the federal government, despite the fact that there have been some six dozen members from Quebec here on a fairly regular basis, plus a Prime Minister from Quebec, all of whom have been unable to cure this alienation and have even made it worse through their frequent tendency toward confrontation and arrogance. This has encouraged a negative attitude to our federal institutions instead of making

people understand the positive side of federalism, people are now probably going to accuse me of siding with it. No, Mr. Speaker. Once more I want to ask this government which has such a strong contingent, at least in numbers, of members from Quebec, to make a last attempt to explain to Quebec government representatives the scope of the fiscal arrangements or at least discuss certain objectives that could be better pursued jointly instead of duplicating our efforts.
I earnestly hope that the impact of this legislation will not cause too much hardship in my home province. I also hope that the government will act on the request I made today that it increase its negotiations and strengthen its relations with the provinces instead of dropping negotiations entirely and denying their importance in order to justify unilateral action, which is altogether undesirable. Increasingly, I have the impression that this government wants to act unilaterally, and I insist, and I cannot say it often enough, that this is not the way to strengthen this country. If we really want to keep alienating Canadians from the federal system, we should go on doing what we are doing now, but if we really want to strengthen this country, if we want to make all Canadians, wherever they happen to be, benefit from federal negotiations with the provinces, there must be a change in attitude and there must be a change soon.
The atmosphere in this Parliament has become an atmosphere of mistrust. Provincial premiers, unions and members of the business world are finding it very difficult to trust this government today. This is an extremely negative factor in view of the present economic situation. If we really want to turn around the economy, I would urge the government to respect the status of the provinces and to make an unprecedented effort to get them to work together with him. I wonder whether the Prime Minister is really interested in getting together with the provinces and working with them. If he is not, Mr. Speaker, I think he should be prepared to make a decision, and it should be that the interests of this country must take precedence over his own interests and objectives. I hope hon. members and ministers on the opposite side will take this opportunity to remind the Prime Minister that his principal role is to unite this country and to help the provinces, and in a federal system, this means supporting the efforts and priorities of the provinces. I feel that these priorities are not incompatible with our greater national objectives. Mr. Speaker, I hope that the arguments, speeches and comments that have been made in connection with Bill C-97 will at least have had the effect of reminding the members of this government that consultation and federal-provincial relations are of paramount importance, now more than ever before. I hope that the recommendations I am making today will be taken seriously, because in making them, I am convinced, with all the sincerity of which any member here is capable, that our country and our provinces will be the better for increased consultation, which in my view is absolutely necessary.

Mr. Speaker, I will not use this opportunity in debate on third reading to go over once again the arguments I have made earlier. I will not go into the argument about the revenue guarantee again, for instance, because I believe that even in the short time provided to the opposition for debating the bill, we have succeeded in getting across to the public what has been going on and what kind of dishonesty the government is involved in when it says that it is only cutting the revenue guarantee and is not cutting money for health care and post-secondary education. We have made the case on the basis of the government's own contention over the last five years about the revenue guarantee, that it is cutting money for health care and post-secondary education. That will become more clear as events unfold when the new fiscal arrangements come into force and people see the effect the cutbacks will have on health care and post-secondary education.
Neither will I go into the argument about the way Manitoba is treated in the new equalization formula embodied in Bill C-97. I will not go into that because I still entertain a hope, however fading at this point, that before the end of the day we may yet see an amendment offered by the government to redress in some way the injustice done to Manitoba in this formula.
April 5, 1982

Rather than repeat the arguments already made-although it is tempting to do so-I want to reflect on our medicare system and some of its problems, in particular the growing unhapiness of the doctors within medicare. We know that there is a dispute in Manitoba between the government and the doctors about the role of binding arbitration, fees and the whole negotiating process. We also know that there is a dispute in Ontario. It seems that in one province after another there is a crisis in the relationship between doctors and the provincial governments and between doctors and medicare as such. I should like to make some observations about that and hope that they will prove helpful to the government.
1 agree with the Canadian Medical Association's contention that medicare is underfunded. I think I should say at the beginning that there are areas of agreement between the New Democratic Party and the Canadian Medical Association. Some time ago I took the time to read the text of an address by the president of the Canadian Medical Association to the St. John's Rotary Club on February 25, 1982. I should like to make a few observations about that speech.
Before I comment on those areas on which I think there is common ground between the CM A and the NDP, 1 should like to refer to an anxiety that was expressed by the president of the CMA at the commencement of his address. He speculated that the audience might well be expected to perceive his remarks as being just one more pitch for higher fees and higher incomes for doctors. I think he put his finger on the impotence, the powerlessness, of the Canadian Medical Association's attempt to alert Canadians to the dangers of prolonged underfunding of our health care system. Why is it that no one seems to listen to the Canadian Medical Association? The fact is that otherwise legitimate concerns of the medical profession are compromised by the consistent link which doctors make between the underfunding of health care, on the one hand, and their incomes, on the other hand.
Having travelled across the country with the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements last year and listened to many different groups concerned with, and/or employed in, our health care system, I regret to say that it was only the doctors who came before the committee in the public hearings to talk about their own incomes. It was as if higher incomes for physicians would somehow solve all problems; as if higher incomes for physicians would mean more chronic care beds; as if higher incomes for physicians would mean more modernized equipment and facilities in hospitals; and as if higher incomes for physicians would mean more nurses in hospitals.
What has also compromised the concern of the medical profession about medicare and about underfunding is the obvious philosophical hostility which some of its spokesmen display toward medicare. One gets the feeling that higher incomes would satisfy some of the discontent in the medical profession but that for another, more vocal group-I would suggest a minority-the root of the problem is medicare itself. It is as if they object to the very principles of medicare and therefore look for every opportunity to discredit the system.

I believe the vast majority of Canadians regard medicare as one of the great post-war achievements in social policy. They cannot be blamed if they are unmoved by, somewhat skeptical of and suspicious about the concern of doctors for medicare, given the criticism that is sometimes heaped on medicare in principle by certain spokespersons for the medical profession.
In my view, the problems of how much physicians ought to be paid and what the mechanism ought to be for determining their income in detail after a general level is set, desperately need to be dealt with, but they must be dealt with separately from the issue of the general underfunding of hospital care or the need for other improvements in our health care system. In this respect I think it can be fairly charged that the medical profession is making the medicare crisis and the debate about medicare more difficult by constantly clouding more important issues with their own self-interest and with their rhetoric about the decline in physicians' incomes. This rhetoric, Mr. Speaker, usually employs 1971 income as the base, without ackowledg-ing that this represents a considerable increase over premedicare income. I pointed this out to the president of the Canadian Medical Association when I wrote to him some weeks ago.
An article appeared in today's The Globe and Mail entitled "Shed No Tears for MDs". It points out that it is misleading to show only what has happened to doctors" incomes since 1971. Indeed, they seem to have gone down since 1971, but it is misleading to use that year as a base because, prior to then, the incomes of doctors were considerably lower. If the truth be told, what happened was that in the years just prior to medicare when they could see medicare coming, physicians' fees started to go up. This was to ensure that when medicare did arrive, the public would be paying these higher fees. The doctors had not charged them until they could see medicare coming. I have heard medicare described not so much as medicare but doctor care. In other words, it ensures that doctors will receive an income from each and every patient dealt with.
I was pleased to see in the presentation of the Canadian Medical Association to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs that for once it made an argument about what was happening to medicare and to patient care and left out the argument about physicians' incomes. If this is an indication that the Canadian Medical Association is moving away from trying to blend these two issues in what I have already said is a very unhelpful way, then I welcome it. I think the two matters need to be dealt with separately, if possible.
The CMA is quite correct in pointing out that Canada spends less of its GNP on health care than many other nations. For instance, the United States spends some 2 per cent more of its GNP on health care. This is not in itself evidence of underfunding in Canada. There are millions of poor Americans who have little or no access to the kind of health care to which

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
almost all Canadians are accustomed, despite the fact that Americans spend 2 per cent more of their GNP on it. The higher costs in the United States are as much the result of higher physicians' incomes and irrational technological competition between unco-ordinated private health centres, as any greater commitment to health care.
The fact that we are spending 2 per cent less of our GNP on health care gives cause for reflection on just how badly health care costs in Canada are rising. We have heard much concern about rising health care costs. Sometimes the concern is tied to the fact that our health care system is being funded publicly which, according to certain ideologues on the right, is a guaranteed way to have higher costs. The fact of the matter is that with a publicly-funded system we in Canada have a much more cost-efficient health care system than the Americans who do it entirely through the private sector. Nevertheless, I agree more support is needed for health care in Canada, not less. This is why my party and I strenuously oppose the proposed cutbacks in federal transfer payments to the provinces.
Furthermore, New Democrats across the country have been vigilant in their opposition to spending restraint in health care practised by most provincial governments since block funding was introduced in 1977. We have been active in relating to the Canadian public the kinds of service deficiencies which the Canadian Medical Association eloquently pointed out in its presentation to the Finance committee or indeed whenever it has the opportunity to do so. No party has a better record of providing facilities and required staff for better chronic health care than that accomplished by various NDP provincial governments in the construction of nursing homes; for instance, my home province of Manitoba comes to mind.
In attempting to provide more public money for such needs, we often run into the opposition of none other than those who now like to lament the inadequacies of medicare. The political right is opposed to increases in government spending and to a more equitable and fair tax system because it thinks that would somehow eliminate incentives and not create the correct investment climate. It is opposed to the measures with which we could pay for increased spending, but at the same time expresses concern about cutbacks in funding for these particular programs.
This is my problem with the approach of hon. members of the Progressive Conservative Party to the issue. I have been happy to have them as allies in opposing the withdrawal of the revenue guarantee, but at this point in the debate I must confess a certain amount of skepticism about the position they take. What is true is that day after day, year after year, they have been instrumental in developing a paranoia about government deficits, upon which the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) now plays as a justification for cutbacks in these programs. I say to the colleagues on my right that they are not without blame or totally non-culpable in the matter. Many of their provincial colleagues are even more to blame.
There is a kind of inconsistency in the approach of the Progressive Conservative Party to the issue. I ask them, in as generous a spirit as I am capable of, to reflect on the contradictions in the rhetoric, on the one hand, about reducing
government spending and, on the other hand, about condemning the government whenever it reduces its spending. We in this corner can at least say that we are consistent. We condemned the government for reducing its spending in this area, and we say that if it means the government has to collect more money in order to fund particular services, we will support it. This is something which hampers the credibility of the Conservative party when it comes to medicare; it is no secret that it is not one of its strong points. There is not a great deal of deep-seated trust among Canadians when it comes to the relationship or the attachment of the Conservative party to medicare.
The underfunding problem in medicare is related to the larger political and economic problem that in a period of shrinking economic growth we must have a greater sharing of our common wealth of such things as health care if we are to maintain and, indeed one could argue, to restore standards. We in the NDP are in favour of a greater sharing of our common wealth. We would be prepared to reform our tax systems in order to make it possible. Is the Canadian Medical Association prepared to advance the argument that those people who made exorbitant incomes last year but paid no taxes at all should be more fairly taxed and should pay their share? Is the CMA prepared to advance the argument that corporations which do not pay their fair share of taxes should pay more taxes in order to fund the health care system? It seems to me that this is the route which must be taken, particularly in these difficult economic times. Are Conservatives prepared to advance a fair and more progressive tax system? 1 do not think so, because every time anybody so much as breathes about reforming the tax system, they are up on their feet talking about the investment climate. It seems that in order to please members of the Progressive Conservative Party when it comes to the tax system, we have to guarantee people can make as much money as they want and then they will do us the favour of doing business in the country; that is not our approach to the tax system.
When it comes to the medicare debate, it is important for people in obvious positions of leadership to be philosophically honest, whether it is the Canadian Medical Association or anyone else. If they are in favour of medicare as a system, then in my opinion they should be advocating more public and political commitment to an appropriate amount of government support, not advocating short-term measures such as more extra billing, a user fee here or charging more for hospital care there. Short-term solutions which introduce private mechanisms for funding added costs of health care in difficult economic times are shortsighted and will destroy medicare as Canadians now understand it. So when the Canadian people can believe that the Canadian Medical Association is unreservedly committed to the survival of medicare and its basic principles, then perhaps others concerned about health care will be able to join hands with the CMA in co-operative action to make sure all Canadians have the best possible health care system and the best possible health, in a system which does not use doctors or anyone else as scapegoats, one in which
April 5, 1982

there is an appropriate balance between the professional integrity and the freedom of doctors and the responsibility of the community to ensure that the allocation of medical resources, scarce or otherwise, is an accountable community decision and not something left to the marketplace.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), Mr. Speaker, now says that she wants to bring in a Canada health act. I hope she means that she wants to develop a new fiscal arrangement for health care superior to the one we had up until today, and superior to the one we will have after third reading of Bill C-97. It seems to me that the fiscal arrangements for health and education get worse every time they are renegotiated, although you cannot say of this one that it was renegotiated because it was unilateral. I hope she has it in mind to bring all existing legislation under one act which will involve certain standards and conditions having to be met in order for provinces to receive federal money. One of the things I hope will be in that new act is the prohibition of extra billing by physicians, and a mechanism to ensure that provinces see to it that there is no extra billing in their jurisdiction.
The medical profession has some arguments in favour of extra billing. They talk about the doctor-patient relationship and the need for a cash transaction in order to enhance the integrity of that relationship. I guess it is only coincidence that this argument is advanced more strenuously the more doctors feel their incomes are not keeping up to what they think they should be. We did not hear that argument as much when doctors were satisfied with their incomes. I guess their relationships with patients had more integrity then. In any case, we hear more now the argument that what is at stake is that relationship and somehow the transfer of money between the doctor and his patient makes the relationship more worth while.
Mr. Speaker, I am only being partly facetious when I say that this sounds like an argument by analogy for the virtues of prostitution: something is only worth while when there is a cash transaction. I question the value of that argument. It sounds good on the surface, but the minute you begin to look at it, it sort of falls away, besides which it is an insult to all the professions who do not operate on a fee-for-service basis. The argument advanced by the CMA concerning the need for money in order to enhance their doctor-patient relationships is, by implication, a charge against the value of the relationships other professionals have where they do not charge on a fee-for-service basis.

Clergymen do not charge per sermon, Mr. Speaker. We just give freely of our time.
Enough said about medicare, Mr. Speaker. I just wanted to put on the record some of the concerns I have over the arguments advanced by the doctors. I do not think doctors are somehow sacred, and I do not think it should be regarded as such a nasty thing to get up here and question some of the arguments they advance about their incomes and their position in medicare. They are answerable to the political process and to public dialogue, just like anyone else. It seems to me that some of them would like to escape that kind of accountability, but there is no retreat from the fact that everyone, doctors, lawyers and everyone else, will have to be more and more accountable if we are serious about the democratization of society. People will have to be accountable for their decisions and not be able to hide behind professional privilege or whatever. That is true not only of doctors but all professions, and it is something we have to keep in mind.
There has been a deterioration in the respect that people have for all professions, for teachers and lawyers. Of course, they have always had a certain disrespect for lawyers, which is a healthy thing. However, this has been happening to all professions in general, which I think is probably a good thing, and doctors should not feel as though they have been singled out. Rather, they should see what is happening to them in the larger social perspective and not blame medicare or any other system as the cause of their problems.
I would like to make a few remarks concerning post-secondary education, the other aspect to the funding that we are concerned about when we talk about federal-provincial fiscal arrangements under the established programs financing act.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Many students, and others, have a growing anxiety concerning the future of post-secondary education. In part there is a feeling that university education does not provide the kind of opportunity it once did. Of course, many think that it still does provide opportunity. But, at one time, it was a truism to say that a university education provided upward mobility, particularly for those who came from a lower-income group or those down the socioeconomic ladder, so to speak. It was the means whereby they could proceed to greater and greater things.
What has happened is that we have begun to realize two things. First, it has not been as great an instrument of social mobility as we would like to believe. When we consider who is attending university, we find there has not been as much progress as we would like to think. For instance, we have not ensured that people from working class backgrounds would actually make it into university in significant numbers. And, even if they do get there, they do not have as much of a guarantee as in the past that a university education will be the means to achieve a success story, or however one wants to describe it.
I think that over the years we have placed too much emphasis on education as a means to provide a greater standard of living and income. Now when we have reached the point at which that can no longer be said to be the case, we find there is a crisis in the perception of post-secondary education.
Unfortunately, I think the government is operating out of this crisis perception. I think that the government has been hinting, as is evident by some of the rhetoric in the debate over post-secondary education, that it wants post-secondary education to be even more instrumental in its view than it has been up until now. It wants to tie the goals of the post-secondary educational community to the needs of the economy.
Of course, no one wants to say that our education system should be independent of the needs of the economy. However, what we and many in the post-secondary educational community are concerned about, and rightly so, is that the government will take an overly instrumental view of post-secondary education. We fear that the government will merely see postsecondary education as a form of manpower training, and that over the years it will begin to underfund those aspects of postsecondary education which are valuable in and of themselves. Those are the aspects which help to create the critical minds which can provide the kind of intelligent and reflective debate which is so necessary to the ongoing health of the political life of a democracy. This is the long-term consideration.
I become very concerned when I hear the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) discussing a voucher system whereby the federal government would actually pull money from the general funding for post-secondary education and give it to students, as individuals, in the form of vouchers. I last heard this advocated by the libertarians during the provincial election in Manitoba in 1969. I thought it was sort of a fringe idea. However, it now seems that it is being actively considered by the federal government.
What would happen in that case? The federal government could then discriminate against those courses that it felt were not as useful to the economy or to its political future. If one wanted courses for a high-tech job, one could receive a voucher of $5,000; but if one wanted to take philosophy, one would only receive $5. This is what I am talking about. It would give the federal government an incredible amount of manipulative power and should cause us grave concern.
We do, however, support the desire of the Secretary of State to have more national dialogue about the role of post-secondary education. In this respect, I do not quite understand why the government will not agree to something like, or identical to, a royal commission on the role of post-secondary education, what the CAUT called for, the equivalent of the first Hall report with regard to post-secondary education. Instead, the government wants to do the same thing it does concerning nuclear power and everything else one can imagine. It wants to have its own little, internal kind of inquiry where one never gets to see the terms of reference, one never gets to hear what the government is thinking or proposing, and then it shows up with a bill one day and gives the House a couple of weeks in which to pass it.
The government would have the support of many people in trying to develop more of a national discussion about the role of post-secondary education. For this reason, I agree with the task force proposal that the funding for health care and postsecondary education be separated so that we could have separate discussions. It is very difficult to tell what the government is spending on each when they are both lumped together in such a way. It also blurs the lines of accountability.
I hope the government will actively consider, at some point in the future, the creation of separate fiscal arrangements for health care and post-secondary education. In relation to health care standards, it should ensure a mechanism whereby the federal government could bring delinquent provinces into line.
It seems to me that this is probably an historic low point for federal-provincial fiscal arrangements as they pertain to health care and post-secondary education. I hope we have sort of bottomed out and that, from here on in, we can begin the process of putting into place a better fiscal arrangement for health care and post-secondary education.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, third reading of Bill C-97, respecting federal-provincial fiscal arrangements and established programs financing, provides the last chance to record, for public attention, the fear and concern that these new measures will adversely affect health, education and other social services across Canada. The debate on Bill C-97 and the limited opportunity for public representations before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs have made it abundantly clear that the changes in equalization provisions and in federal contributions to established services will seriously affect the financial ability of many provinces to continue all government services at current levels and standards.
April 5, 1982

It is unfortunate, as we meet today, that we are under the directive from the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) that, unless this bill is passed, the financial provisions and the provinces affected by them will be endangered. It was with that threat hanging over our heads that we hastened to complete deliberations on this bill which will have such far-reaching effects for the provinces and for the residents of those provinces which are dependent upon transfer payments for their very financial existence.
The government's claim is that $105 billion will be transferred to the provinces over the next five years to support equalization and established programs, principally, health care and post-secondary education. The Minister of Finance tells us that this amount is substantially larger than the $61 billion transferred to the provinces for equalization and established programs in the five years ending March 31, 1982.
While the proposed contribution appears generous, let us remember the rate at which total federal expenditures have increased over the years. For the fiscal year 1980-1981, total federal expenditures were $58.6 billion. Five years later, for fiscal year 1985-86, total federal expenditures are forecast to reach $105 billion. As a result, federal expenditures will almost double in five years.
It is not surprising, then, that an increase from $61 billion to $105 billion for federal transfer payments to provinces for a subsequent five-year period might result in less real financial support to the provinces. The important bottom line on the government's new proposals contained in Bill C-97 is the net effect or result on provincial finances.
It has been said time and time again in this debate, but never has it been denied, that the net effect or result on all of the provinces collectively is that federal transfer payments will be reduced in this five-year period commencing April 1, 1982, by $5.7 billion. That is, the federal treasury will be saved $5.7 billion by applying the new formulas enacted by Bill C-97. To take Nova Scotia as an example, Mr. Speaker, this change will result in a decrease in revenues from transfer payments of at least $100 million and possibly an amount as high as $200 million. If you transpose that into the population available to support the revenues of the province of Nova Scotia, it means an additional amount per taxpayer of almost $300. If you spread it across the whole population over that time frame, of course the amount is less; but we have to recognize that it is only from the taxpayers that the government can obtain revenues. The result of this saving to the federal government is a deficit to the provinces that receive transfer payments, and that eventually will have to be passed on to the residents and citizens of those provinces.
Who can quarrel, Mr. Speaker, with an attempt by the Government of Canada to reduce its massive deficit, a deficit which has been running close to $10 billion annually and a public debt in excess of $128 billion that soaks up one dollar in every four revenue dollars? That is a deficit and public debt
Federal Transfers to Provinces
that costs each and every Canadian $4,900, and that costs each and every taxpayer approximately $ 12,500.
What we can and should bring to public attention, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that the Government of Canada is reducing its deficit by withdrawing financial assistance to the provinces to the extent of $5.7 billion in a five-year period. At the same time, the federal government is virtually forcing those provinces to keep and maintain the same level and standard of public services that it has asked and encouraged the provinces to provide for its residents to ensure national standards in health, education and social assistance.
The federal government, having established the level and standard of government services to Canadians, now seeks to abandon part of its financial responsibility for the provision of these services. "Co-operative federalism" is indeed dead in Canada, Mr. Speaker. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made that pronouncement a few weeks ago, he was not really stating a fact but was making the announcement that he and his government had killed "co-operative federalism". It was, in a word, Mr. Speaker, homicide and not suicide. The Prime Minister must take the responsibility for the ultimate result.
This country has grown on the basis of co-operation between the federal government and the provincial governments to achieve programs and services that are available to all Canadians. The statement that co-operative federalism is dead endangers that process and the procedure by which these programs and services were made available to Canadians in the past.
It is essential to underline and clarify the effect of the cutback of $5.7 billion in transfer payments to the provinces.
Faced with a substantial loss in revenue, these provinces have only four alternatives. First, the provinces may use other revenues or untapped sources of revenue to provide for the loss of revenue. An important footnote to that alternative is that most provinces operate on an annual deficit and do not have the resources available to them. Other provinces have virtually exhausted their sources of revenue.
A second alternative would be to reduce or cut back services. We cannot do this in the fields of medical and health care because of the great danger it would pose to the persons who receive benefit from those services. By the same token, the universities, and the students who attend those universities and other post-secondary institutions, would be horrified by the prospect of cutting back services and programs within those institutions.
The third alternative I want to outline is that provinces have the alternative of reducing standards of services. Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone in this House or any responsible elected official across Canada would favour a reduction in the standard of services, particularly in the health care and educational fields.
The fourth alternative left to the provinces, Mr. Speaker, is to increase taxation. Some provinces, like Nova Scotia and Ontario, are more or less at the end of the line with respect to taxation.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
In a moment, Mr. Speaker, I want to provide some information on the extent to which the provinces have exhausted their tax resources. First, I want to say that if none of these alternatives that I have outlined is readily available, medical doctors, hospitals, universities, colleges and other post-secondary institutions are left with resolving the problem within the framework of their own institutions and within the framework of their own practices. They must consider cutting back these services or reducing the standards of those services. In the end, whether it is the provinces that make the decision in terms of cutting back or reducing services, or in terms of imposing taxes, or whether it is the deliverers of those services themselves, the medical doctors, the hospitals, the universities and post-secondary institutions, the public across Canada are affected. It will be the people of Canada that will either bear the increased cost or suffer from the cutbacks and reductions in services. The point is that in the case of the provincial governments which cannot raise revenues or tap sources of revenues, the only alternative left to them in many cases is cutbacks in services or reductions in the standard of those services.
Let me speak now, Mr. Speaker, about provincial taxes and our increase in provincial taxes as a means of making up the deficit which the federal government has imposed on the provinces to the extent of $5.7 billion in the next five years. It has already been reported that many of the provinces simply do not have any further tax base to use. In fact, the survey included with the budget documents which the minister brought to the House of Commons on November 12, 1981, indicated that on a scale of 100, two provinces, Nova Scotia and Ontario, only rank 88; that is to say, they have exhausted their resources and taxation capabilities to that extent. In contrast, the province of Alberta has a score of 192, so it is easy to see that this particular province, in relation to the provinces of Ontario and Nova Scotia, does have some resources which it might apply to make up any deficit in transfer payments.
I might mention for the record, Mr. Speaker, that among the other Atlantic provinces in which I have a particular interest, New Brunswick rated an 89 in relation to the base figure 100, Newfoundland rated 92, and Prince Edward Island, 97. You can see that those provinces have little capability to make up any deficit that results from cutbacks in federal transfer payments.
The other aspect of increasing taxes as a method to meet any shortfall imposed by the Government of Canada is the capability of the taxpayers, residents in each province, to bear additional taxes. I have a report that indicates that today 41 per cent of a family's income is expended for taxes, apart from food and shelter. Those figures indicate, if I were to list them, that among the people of Canada there is very little room left for payment of increased taxes. For instance, the average British Columbia family will earn $29,201 this year and will have to pay $12,114 of that to governments. Income tax is the biggest single item at $4,055. The myriad of other taxes account for the other $8,059. When an average family in British Columbia with an income of $29,201 pays $12,114 in
federal income tax and a myriad of other taxes, we realize that the taxpayers of Canada have pretty well reached their limit.
With rising costs for food, shelter, transportation and other essential services, each day erodes the ability of the Canadian public to put more money into taxes to pay for services they have been receiving in the past. It is not a simple matter, as the Minister of Finance may claim, to allow the federal government to get rid of its deficit by transferring the problem to the provinces and then have the provinces utilize their resources to acquire additional funds to apply to the shortfall. As I have already explained, in the case of most provinces, certainly the Atlantic provinces, that involves increased taxation. There is simply no room for that either in terms of the financial capacity to raise additional taxes or the financial capacity of the people to pay additional taxes.
What the federal government has left us, with its financial policy and the provisions of Bill C-97, is a problem that appears to be insoluble. It can be resolved only by a reduction of services or a change in the standards of those services.
In the debate on Bill C-97 in this House and in the committee which reviewed this bill and heard public representations with respect to its provisions, there has been myriad statistical information and a plethora of financial information. I am not going to add to that.
We have in addition the report of the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal earnings. It also contains a great deal of information on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements in the past and makes recommendations for the future. My major purpose is to consider the human side of the fiscal reductions proposed by Bill C-97 and to indicate the effect these reductions will have on Canadians.
We have the Canadian dream of equal services across Canada in the essential areas of health, education and social services. Previous Liberal governments, and politicians in this House and elsewhere across this country have attempted to establish national standards in essential services so that as you go from province to province in Canada, each citizen receives the same standard and level of basic services. That dream is in danger today. Once having been established and implemented across this country, the Government of Canada threatens that dream; it threatens to destroy that dream that has become a reality over the past decade.
I want to deal, in this context of the human side and the effect on human beings, with the matter of the equalization payments that are made to those provinces which cannot, according to financial tests, provide services at the level that the richer provinces of Canada are able to do. I also want to talk about health care, including medical and hospital care, and post-secondary education.
First I want to consider why the Government of Canada has taken this drastic action at this stage in our development and is cutting back on the amount of its transfer payments to those provinces which require the payments to provide services.
April 5, 1982

Why, in 1982, does the government see fit to do this in the face of all kinds of economic difficulties and massive unemployment, approaching 1.2 million persons unemployed? In addition, there are 250,000 no longer looking for work. Another
260,000	are employed at jobs much below their level of capability and qualification. Approximately 1.5 million Canadians are employed part-time. When you add all that up, you find almost three million Canadians have an employment problem. There are grave difficulties across the country. This affects the whole fabric of our society. In the face of that, the government has decided to cut back on the payments to provinces used to provide essential services to their citizens.
We must ask ourselves why the Government of Canada is taking this action at this time. I can only answer in this way. There appear to be two developments that have led to the introduction of Bill C-97 and the change of attitude on the part of the Government of Canada respecting financial transfers to the provinces. One development is quite specific. It is the financial plan contained in the budget introduced November 12, 1981. That budget proposed as its main thrust to restrain government spending and reduce the deficit. As a second prong of that thrust, the government purported to apply equity to the tax measures that comprise our tax system. I will talk about that in a moment.
The second development is much more unjustifiable. I refer to the increase in the hostility of the federal government to provincial governments and the complaint by the federal government that it does not receive political credit from the provincial governments for the services it provides and for the financial payments it makes to the provinces to provide other services. That is an important development when you consider that in all ten provinces there does not exist such a thing as a Liberal government. One can easily see why there is this hostility toward the provincial governments.
One wonders why the Government of Canada would take steps to enact measures in this House of Commons through the budget and through Bill C-97 which wreak havoc with those provincial governments in their financial dealings. The reason has been stated by the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) in public on at least two or three occasions that I am aware of; they are upset about this lack of political credit. The Secretary of State was quoted in the February 22, 1982, edition of the Toronto Star. That newspaper is not known for giving support to the opposition parties in this House of Commons. That newspaper saw fit to report remarks made by the Secretary of State. The article stated, and I quote:
From now on, Ottawa wants to get direct political credit for whatever it spends, whether it's in a federal or provincial jurisdiction, and is prepared to go around the provinces by giving universities or students direct aid, if it can't make a new deal with the provincial governments.
The article also stated:
If the Government of Canada is to remain relevant to the citizens of the country, it must deal more directly with the citizens, or must have the citizens realize what it is doing or how their dollars are being spent and not merely be a banker for the provinces-
That is what the Secretary of State said in an interview with the Toronto Star. The federal government just cannot be a
Federal Transfers to Provinces
banker, it has to get credit. The people of Canada have to know what it is doing with their tax dollars. They have to know it is helping to finance hospital and medical care, and that university students are being assisted by the Government of Canada.
To get that political credit, to get that silly point across to the people of Canada, that is what it is doing. As if Canadians did not know from the payment of their taxes that the government is receiving vast amounts of money! To get that little point across, the federal government is setting about endangering the whole federal-provincial system, merely to gain some credit.
We have these two developments. One is very serious, if misguided, in terms of the budget provisions. The second is the search for political credit which has led to the introduction of Bill C-97 and this change in federal-provincial fiscal relations.
Let me talk briefly about the budget which, as I have indicated, has the intention of reducing the federal deficit and allegedly bringing equity to the tax system. I stated that the Minister of Finance claims to have reduced the federal deficit, but we have already seen, as evidenced by Bill C-97, that all the Minister of Finance has done is taken the $5.7 billion which should have gone to the provinces under the existing cost-sharing and transfer formulae and kept it in the hands of the federal government. He simply grabbed the $5.7 billion which will eventually be applied to the federal deficit through the government's financing process.
That is why the Economic Council of Canada has said that the budget does not, in fact, contain measures which will effectively reduce the deficit and restore faith in the government's financial capability. That is why the Economic Council of Canada has pointed out time and again and confirmed that what is occurring is simply a transfer of the deficit from the federal government to the provincial governments. This cannot be of any possible financial benefit to the people of this nation.
This leads us to examine another justification which was given for the budget. It is that the tax measures were intended to create equity. I will list only a few of those measures. For example, there is the loss of the pension deduction. This has a detrimental effect on senior Canadians who should be given some encouragement to provide for the years when they will not be able to work by saving during their working life. They are being punished for their endeavours by having the pension deduction taken away from them if they receive pension income and continue to work. That is the minister's attitude toward the senior citizens of this country.
Another provision of the budget is to tax health benefit plans which were introduced by employers with the co-operation and consent of employees to ensure the employees receive adequate health services. The Canadian government will now tax the employer's contribution to those programs resulting in the fear that those programs may collapse simply because employees are unwilling to pay tax on dollars that they do not
