even receive. Who can blame the seven million employed people across Canada who participate in the health benefit plans but do not receive any money, only to be asked by the federal government to pay tax on the dollars that they do not receive? That is what the Minister of Finance does to the working people of Canada.
There are 13 million Canadians who have life insurance in order to provide for their families in the event of an untimely death or physical disability. With respect to life insurance, the Minister of Finance will tax that desire to protect their families from unfortunate accidents.
Workers' benefits will be taxed in a manner different from that which was applied in the past. Those workers who are employed in northern Canada's frontier or offshore and receive food, clothing and shelter or are provided with transportation in the course of their work will now be taxed on a much stricter basis and will be required to pay more tax. How will that attitude of the government help the development of northern Canada and help Canada grow and develop its resources which have been neglected?
Other Canadians who will be affected are the farmers and fishermen who work all their lives to build up their equity in a farm or a fishing vessel. The only way they can provide for their future is to sell their assets-whether it is a farm or a fishing vessel-and put the money which they receive into an income-averaging annuity to avoid having it taxed at the highest possible rate in the year in which they receive it, so that their future security will not be wiped away. The minister will not allow farmers and fishermen and small businessmen, who have used this device in the past, to use it any longer. He is taking it away. Where is the equity in that?
Those are only some examples which prove the falsehood of the budget. There is the falsehood expressed by Bill C-97 that the government is restraining its expenditures and bringing equity into the tax system. We are left with Bill C-97 and its cutbacks which will affect Canadians for the next five years. Co-operative federalism is indeed dead. It has been killed by this budget and by the Prime Minister, who will not consider the reality that Canadians need services and an effective system to provide financially for those services.
The net result of the budget is that the federal government receives more and the provincial governments receive less. However, the provincial governments are still faced with the necessity of providing essential and necessary services to their citizens. The federal government has abandoned Canadians in all provinces and is not providing the provinces with the financial capability to provide services.
As I have indicated, the Secretary of State supports this legislation in the wake of the failure of the provinces to give political credit to the Government of Canada for the role that it plays. How callous and mean can you get when you are dealing with your own electorate, the people of Canada, who have elected this government? Canadians should be annoyed at how they are being treated. Many Canadians do not understand what is occurring in the House of Commons. They do not always understand the effect of the budget provisions or the effect of a piece of legislation like Bill C-97. That is why
we stand in the House and before committees, like my colleague for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) did, and try to get the message across to the government and Canadians about the harmful effects of these financial measures. That is why we try to prevent the government from hiding behind an alleged policy of fiscal restraint or an alleged policy of equity in its budget measures.
We want to expose the government so that Canadians will be able to judge their elected representatives on both sides of the House and will be able to render judgment when the time comes. In the meantime, we will not listen to the fabrications foisted on the House by the government that it is restraining expenditures and creating equity in the tax system, while at the same time allowing essential services to be provided to Canadians in the same manner as in the past.
We must consider Bill C-97 in the context of the financial situation in Canada. We realize that the government has already spent too much of the taxpayers' money for too long and has piled up deficits which are too high. These deficits are coming back to haunt Canadians and particularly the Government of Canada. We must maintain services which we all regard as essential to all Canadians. I can think of many ways to raise the funds to support those services. All you have to do is look at the $500 million dollar deficit in the Post Office. There are $675 million in debt write-offs for the St. Lawrence Seaway. It is not difficult to find funds that will allow the government to maintain transfer payments at the current level so as to preserve the capability of the provinces to provide these services. Even if the government is not willing to do this for all the provinces which have been receiving transfer payments, at least it can do it in the case of those provinces, such as the maritime provinces, which it knows are unable to provide the financing for these essential services.
Now that the Minister of Finance has entered the chamber, I will remind him that the government of Nova Scotia, for example, already has a deficit of $200 million; Newfoundland has a deficit approaching that amount, as has the government of New Brunswick. In percentage terms, the government of Prince Edward Island has a similar deficit.
1 also want to remind the minister that these provinces are already spending a large amount of their total revenue on social services, education, and health. In Newfoundland, 25 per cent of the provincial revenue is spent on education, 20.6 per cent is spent on health and 17.9 per cent is spent on other social services. Where is that province's capacity to continue to provide services at current levels without help from the federal government? I remind the minister that I have already indicated that the bottom line of this proposal is that $5.7 billion less will be flowing to the provinces, including the Atlantic provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
In the time I have left I would like to deal with the human side of the four elements which are very much involved in Bill C-97, the proposal we now have before us, with respect to
April 5, 1982

federal fiscal transfers to the provinces. As I have indicated, those four points are equalization, health care, medical care, including hospital care and post-secondary education.
First a word about equalization. Equalization in relation to the concept of regional disparity did not just pop out of thin air. It has been a matter of great concern to people in the Atlantic area for some time as well as people in Manitoba and in some parts of western Canada. That is why, when the government brought forward its proposal of a Charter of Rights and Freedoms for all Canadians, we on the east coast were particularly concerned with the inclusion in that Charter of Rights and Freedoms of a provision respecting equalization. That provision was included in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in Section 36. I just want to read Section 36(2) into the record because it states in a few words the concept of equalization. It says:
Parliament and the Government of Canada are committed to the principle of making equalization payments to ensure that provincial governments have sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation.
That is what equalization is, and that is what it states in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
What has happened to that concept? What has happened to that provision in the charter in relation to Bill C-97? The Government of Canada has simply determined in advance that all that that provision, which will be enacted as part of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, means is that the level of services which the Government of Canada plans to support once Bill C-97 goes into effect is sufficient for the purposes of the charter.
Citizens and residents of provinces like Nova Scotia wonder what they are getting in this provision respecting equalization. What are we getting? Are we getting anything or are we not? Is there any meaning to it? Does it change anything? What is the point of the provision if the Minister of Finance and his government can simply come along and change the formula and the provisions for equalization, eliminate the revenue guarantee and change the provisions of the established programs financing and say: "There you have it, ladies and gentlemen, that is it; that is all you get; never mind this constitutional provision?"
It seems awfully funny because in recent years we in eastern Canada, and particularly in Nova Scotia, have looked forward to the future with some hope and expectation because we see offshore developments, and we see a changing attitude on the part of the Government of Canada evidenced by its willingness to include in a constitutional proposal and enshrine into law the right of each province to be equal and to have equal benefits in terms of government services. The duty on the part of the Government of Canada is to eliminate regional disparity. When we see that kind of attitude demonstrated in the provisions of Section 36 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms and when we see the possibility of development of new resources offshore and new revenues from those resources, we have hope for the future. But then that hope is immediately

wiped out in a single act; the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance in November of 1981, and now Bill C-97 which claims for the federal government the right to legislate the rules regardless of the constitutional reference to equalization and regional disparity. That is a great and grave disappointment to us.
I want to talk briefly about health services and first about medicare. We in Canada and certainly in this Parliament sometimes have the idea that we are the prime movers in the health care field and that we are way ahead of the rest of the world when it comes to the provision of health services, either in the form of medical care or hospital care to our citizens. That is simply not true. There are many countries in the world which spend greater percentages of their gross national products on health care services than does Canada. In fact, over the past few years many nations have increased their expenditures on health care services at a greater rate than has Canada. We cannot stand still in these fields. We want for Canadians the best possible health care services, and we have to work to provide those services. Even countries which are often thought of as being less fortunate in terms of social and health services than Canada, such as Saudi Arabia, can claim to have health services, and particularly hospital services, of a high calibre and possibly even higher than those in Canada, so we do not want to go to sleep on this development. We do not want to assume that we have achieved a level of excellence and that we can rest for a while, because that is not true at all. Those in this chamber and across Canada who have had to go to the United States, West Germany and other parts of the world for health services will know that while we have done a very good job-and I commend our medical profession and our hospital operators-we still have a long way to go and cannot relax one bit.
With respect to medicare, I was amazed at the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) with respect to income for medical doctors. The idea that a medical doctor is not entitled to an appropriate and proper income for the services he extends is totally ludicrous.

We are very proud of the doctors we educate in Canada, and we are very proud of the fact that they stay in Canada to administer to the needs of Canadians.
However, at the very same time we have to be very concerned about the number of doctors leaving Canada. In 1977, that number was 549; in 1978, 663; and in 1979, 605. With that number of members of the medical profession leaving Canada we know there must be a problem, and we have to ask ourselves what it is. If the problem is a low level of income to

those doctors or if the problem is a lack of services and facilities available to them, then we have to work to solve that problem because, as the Minister of Finance and everyone in this chamber knows, we spend vast amounts of money educating doctors in Canada. It would be a terrible thing if we allowed ourselves to lose the benefits provided by those people simply because we did not provide for them adequately in terms of finances.
I understood I had 40 minutes and I am coming to the end of that time, but I just want to say a word about hospital care. Again, failure to finance hospital care properly will result in dangers to the health of Canadians. We do not want that. What we have to do in the case both of hospital care and medical care is establish what the standard of service ought to be for all Canadians and, having established that standard, we have to be prepared to pay for it. It is as simple as that and there is no way around it. We have to establish the standard of care and then find the means to pay for it. We cannot blame doctors. We cannot blame hospital authorities. We simply have to deal with the realities of the problem.
Let me talk about post-secondary education in the two minutes I have left. Let us think of the students across Canada whose careers will be in jeopardy if we do not find funds to finance post-secondary education. Again, we have to view the cutbacks with that in mind.
The time has come to face up to the realities of the situation and to find the funds for essential services so that we can help and benefit all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank you for permitting me to participate in the third reading debate on Bill C-97. At this final stage I should like to comment on a number of the points made in the course of the debate and to give my views on a number of concerns raised by hon. members.
First of all, there has been some comment about the length of time allotted to deal with the issues in this particular bill. There has been, however, a good deal more involvement and understanding by members of this House in this debate on fiscal arrangements than there has ever been in the past. This is due, at least in part, to the establishment of the parliamentary task force which has proved to be a major step forward for parliamentary interest in, and parliamentary influence over, federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. Without the work done by the parliamentary task force there would not have been as great an understanding of the issues debated at second reading and in committee. The total debate would not have been as productive. I think all members who participated in the task force headed by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) have acknowledged the value of their involvement.
April 5, 1982

The report of the task force comments on the result of the exercise as follows:
[It] marks the first occasion on which public consultation, and active parliamentary involvement, have been possible during the process of reviewing and renegotiating the central features of fiscal federalism in Canada.
1 should certainly like to thank members of the parliamentary task force from all parties for their valuable contribution. I should also like to thank members who participated in the debate at second reading, at committee stage and at third reading.
1 have noted with satisfaction the general approval given by members of all parties to most elements of the bill. They have not approved all elements, but a substantial number of the important elements have been endorsed. I am pleased to note also the support which has been given to the government's proposals for a new equalization system. This is a program which we all agree is of the utmost importance to our federation.
I am pleased there has been considerable support for the equalization formula given by provincial governments. It has not been possible in every case to meet the concerns of all provincial governments, but I believe that most equalizationreceiving provinces would acknowledge that their views have been listened to on quite a number of important aspects.
I am also pleased to note the support for the continuation and improvement of our fiscal stabilization program. In addition, support has been expressed for the proposal to make over $200 million in payments to fiscally disadvantaged provinces in order to offset the effects of the recoveries of equalization arising from the 1981 census. In that connection I should mention the discussions I had with the representatives of the Atlantic provinces and the province of Manitoba. Certainly in the case of the Atlantic provinces, the arrangement entered into has been of direct benefit. The ministers of the provinces, including the Premier of New Brunswick, have expressed their appreciation of the efforts made to accommodate them in this respect.
Approval has also been given to the proposal to accelerate payments to oil-producing provinces of their share of the federal oil export charge.
There have been criticisms of the bill, of course. Most of these have been directed to the established programs financing provisions. Before I deal with those criticisms, I should like to deal with the case of the province of Manitoba and indicate why it was not possible to accept the proposal to base Manitoba's equalization entitlement on the entitlement of the province with the second lowest rate of growth. Acceptance of this proposal would have meant that the entitlement of one province would have been based upon that of another. The whole idea behind equalization is that it be based upon each province's measure of fiscal capacity. It does not make sense to provide that it could be based upon the fiscal capacity of another province. That has never been the case. If that proposal were adopted, it would go a long way to weakening-I will not say undermining, but to weakening-the credibility of the equalization program. It would be extremely arbitrary.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
We recognized that Manitoba did have a concern and a problem and that what was needed was an arrangement which would protect a province such as Manitoba which would be adversely affected by the change from one equalization system to another. If no steps had been taken to accommodate the concerns of Manitoba, they would have been a drop in the entitlement of Manitoba in the first year of the new five-year period. I believe it would have dropped by 10 per cent over the preceding year. However, on the base of the first year of the new period, its entitlements would have increased in accordance with the more or less general level of increase applicable to all other provinces.
To meet this particular transitional problem we proposed an arrangement with a substantial cost of $165 million over the three years in so far as the province of Manitoba is concerned. This is a very generous provision and is unprecedented in the history of the program. I believe this provision is adequate to meet the circumstances.
Hon. members are aware that the purpose of equalization is to increase the revenue-raising capacity of equalizationreceiving provinces up to the prescribed standard level. We select a standard which we think is fair and adequate and then bring disadvantaged provinces up to that level. The effect of the proposed transitional measure put forward by the government will be that for a period of three years Manitoba's per capita fiscal capacity will be raised to a level higher than that of any of the other provinces that receive equalization. Indeed, in 1982-83 and in 1983-84, Manitoba's fiscal capacity after equalization will be even higher than that of Ontario.
I know that an amendment has been seriously proposed by two members of the House of Commons which would have raised Manitoba's fiscal capacity above that of Ontario for all five years of the new arrangement, even though Ontario would receive no equalization payment. In my view, that would have created real difficulties. It would have been unacceptable from an equalization point of view. The amendment was not acceptable because it was quite costly, but also because it did not make sense in terms of an equalization program which is intended to deal with the fiscal capacity of various provinces. That is my comment about the Manitoba case.
In addition to the recovery provision amounting to $30 million in the case of Manitoba, we have provided a transitional arrangement costing an additional $165 million. In any equalization program, if fiscal capacity related to a standard is to be the guide, provinces will vary in their entitlements. Otherwise it does not make sense as an equalization system.
It is worth recalling, because one does not want a residue of bitterness to prevail, that when we started the last period of equalization the entitlements of the province of Manitoba in comparison with those of the Atlantic provinces were much greater; the percentage rate of growth was more rapid. It is the opposite this time because of the operation of the standard and the fiscal capacity of Manitoba. As the fiscal capacity of a province increases, its entitlements will decrease. The closer a province gets to the standard, the less entitlement it will have;

that is the general system. We have attempted to help Manitoba as a result of discussions which my officials and I have had with the minister of finance.
It has also been suggested in the course of the debate on this bill that the five-province standard proposed for the new equalization formula is inadequate because, "there is no evidence that the five provinces now selected ... are appropriate provinces for a mean average of Canada." I should like to remind hon. members that the five provinces in question, namely Manitoba, Ontario, Quebec, British Columbia and Saskatchewan, account for over 80 per cent of the total provincial population. Moreover, Alberta, which is the largest of the provinces excluded from the standard, certainly cannot be considered as more representative of all provinces than any of the five standard provinces taken individually. Its resource revenues are such that it enjoys a unique position among our ten provinces. As for the four Atlantic provinces excluded from the standard, it should be noted that their inclusion would result in a lower standard than that provided for in the bill.
I will not digress and reflect upon the initial proposal to bring all provinces up to the Ontario standard. I thought that was a good standard. I thought we were hitching the destiny of equalization-receiving provinces to an admirable standard provided by the province of Ontario. But others did not have the confidence in the stability of that province that I had.
Therefore, I moved to a five-province standard which in the view of provincial spokesmen-and their views ought to be respected-would be more stable over the long term. This is why we moved from the Ontario standard to the five-province standard. I must say that almost all equalization-receiving provinces regard the five-province standard as better than the Ontario standard, although I am sure all of them would wish to have kept the pre-existing equalization formula, which in the circumstances was not possible.
Let me say a word on established programs financing, the part of the bill which has been attacked by hon. members of the opposition. Given the quantity of inaccurate information and improbable argument which we have heard in the debate, it seems useful to start with a brief summary of what Bill C-97 proposes to do about established programs financing.
It is not very complicated; there are only two clauses involved. Clause 6 indicates that the total entitlement will be paid as a cash contribution and an equalized tax transfer. That clause goes on to set out the total entitlement of a province as the per capita federal contribution in respect of hospital insurance, medicare and post-secondary education under the cost-sharing arrangements in 1975-76, multiplied by the current year provincial population, and increased by the growth in the Canadian economy. Thus, the total entitlement of a province is based upon the actual experience of 1975-76, escalated by the growth of the Canadian economy. It is worth stressing that federal contributions in 1975-76 represented 100 per cent of the federal contributions under these programs. If 100 per cent of the federal contribution is escalated each year by the growth of the economy, we have a pretty solid base, and the contribution will grow in the future on that solid base.
I have not heard anyone in the opposition criticize any of these elements. Federal contributions under cost-sharing were based upon what it cost to run health insurance and postsecondary education. When the switch was made five years ago from a cost-sharing formula to a block-funding approach, it seemed a fair basis-it still is. Current entitlements, which will go from 1982-83 onward, will start from that base and grow with the population. This is not an unreasonable approach since both health and educational services are supplied to people, people are the population, and the base grows with the population.
Finally, it seems reasonable to assume that federal contributions to these programs should grow in line with the growth of prices and incomes in the country. Using an escalator based upon the gross national product would appear to accomplish this. If all three parts of the total entitlement appear reasonable, it is hard to understand why combining them creates such criticism.
What would opposition members have us do at a time when restraint in federal expenditure is necessary? Is it argued that we should continue a transfer-and this is what it is all about-originally designed to guarantee provincial income tax receipts during implementation of a tax reform ten years ago, the short-term revenue impact of which was difficult to predict? Since the tax change took place ten years ago, the necessary adjustment period must surely be over by now. Is it really necessary to continue, not even the adjustment payment, but a payment designed to cushion the reduction in provincial cash flows which its termination involved? This is the compensation for the termination of the revenue guarantee. A system which is based solidly upon the actual cost experience of 197576, which grows with the population and with the gross national economy, is a very fair way for the Government of Canada to support post-secondary education and health care.
A number of opposition speakers-I gather even today- claim that the cuts are not in transfers to provinces but in transfers to hospitals and universities. They claim the revenue guarantee, which is to be eliminated, was a payment to the hospitals and universities. Well, if that is the case I would like to see the evidence, because it has yet to be produced. The estimates we have produced, which are not disputed, show regular increases in entitlements and transfers. Over the next five years these transfers will increase, as I told the committee, at 12 per cent to 13 per cent-[DOT]

Mr. Speaker, the problems that the opposition complain about so loudly-that is, reduced funding for health and education, increased charges and falling standards-simply cannot be laid on the doorstep of the Government of Canada. Nor can they, under current arrangements, be resolved by the Government of Canada alone.
Having said that, the concerns raised are obviously illegitimate. The standards of health care and post-secondary education in Canada are of concern to all hon. members, and they should continue to be. However, the problems arising from these concerns are in fact the sort of issues that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) hope to redress in their discussions with provincial health and education ministers. The two federal ministers want to be able to assure us, as the task force said they should, that the money voted in this House for health and post-secondary education, and the associated tax revenue we have given up to the provinces, is in fact spent on these services. Those ministers would like to have some input into the planning of progams so that they will reflect, and adjust to, the changing needs of the Canadian economy. It is a fact that we believe our national university system should respond to the needs of our society and our economy. But there is no opportunity, nor has there been in recent years, for any federal minister to participate in any discussions at the council of ministers on these subjects, even though it was clearly understood that this would result from the 1977 negotiations. Provincial ministers have not been prepared to discuss and negotiate our legitimate national concerns about health and education programs.
There is more to this business than money. Money is important, but there is also the necessity for this House to have some assurance that the moneys voted for these purposes are spent on these purposes, and that the universities, which are national institutions, do so. If I may say so personally, it has been a regret of mine that in recent years the universities have appeared more and more to be provincially oriented and drawn more into local and provincial concerns rather than national concerns. To me that would be a rather deplorable development if it continued.

-about the population recovery adjustment payments with which I dealt in Part II of the bill. It has been stated that the provisions pertaining to these payments are unfair because they would preclude the possibility of Saskatchewan receiving payments, although that province will be subject to recoverance. I would like to deal with that because, here again, it is important to make it clear that provinces have been fairly treated.
Why did we bring recovery adjustment payments into the bill? We brought them into the bill because of the financial hardship which would be imposed upon the provinces if we did now what has always been the case; namely, if we went ahead with these recoveries. For example, the finance minister of Newfoundland who, I believe, was faced with recoveries of $60 million to $70 million, would certainly find his budget damaged if we insisted on these recoveries. It was in response to that kind of attitude expressed by him, Premier Hatfield, Mr. Matheson, Mr. MacPhail and Mr. Schroeder, that the effect on their budgets was considered and this provision was included.
The population recovery adjustment payments are designed to ease the financial situation of provinces which meet two criteria. First, they must be subject to population related recoveries of part of the equalization paid to them for fiscal years 1980-81 and 1981-82 as a consequence of new population data contained in the June, 1981, census. Second, they must have below standard fiscal capacity in 1982-1983, an indication that normal recovery procedures would strain their financial situation at the time the recovery would commence. The province of Saskatchewan meets the first requirement but not the second. Indeed, recent calculations based upon the new and improved measure of fiscal capacity, which would underline equalization calculations for the next five years, indicate that Saskatchewan at present has a fiscal capacity which is
quite comparable to that of British Columbia and which is exceeded only by Alberta.
One reason for Saskatchewan's very high capacity is contained in this very bill. Section 10 of the bill provides for the payment of $273 million of shared federal revenues to Saskatchewan in respect of the oil export charge. That is a very large sum for a province of less than one million people. I am glad that it is benefiting from its resources. This is a new source of revenue for Saskatchewan which will buttress existing revenues from royalties to oil, potash, uranium and other minerals from its rich agricultural-based economy.
I should add in passing that a perusal of the budget tabled by the Saskatchewan minister of finance on March 18 gives no indication that population related recoveries of equalization would strain the public finances of that province. That is why a provision has not been put in the bill in the case of Saskatchewan. It is because its fiscal capacity is such that the recoveries would not strain its public finances.
I know that hon. members have been proposing amendments. It has not been possible to accept these amendments because we are attempting to follow a certain strategy of fiscal restraint. We cannot respond to all the requirements of the provinces. However, we do believe that we have provided for an equitable system. We have provided that the payments under the established programs financing for those vital programs for the Canadian people will grow over the next five years at an average rate of 12 per cent to 13 per cent. In this bill, we have enshrined a system of equalization which, I believe, carries the support of most of the equalization receiving provinces.

speechtext:
I listened with a good deal of interest and hope, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when he was speaking, because coming from the province of Manitoba, of course, we as Members of Parliament feel that the people of Manitoba have more than a passing interest in the legislation that we are dealing with at the present time.
I am disappointed that the Minister of Finance really has not said anything new in the way of alleviating the problem that concerns the people of Manitoba.
The minister, at the conclusion of his speech, said that he hoped that this bill would pass and he was sure the provinces would agree with him. But let us take the situation that you were living in the province of Manitoba and had, over roughly a five-year period, a shortfall in revenues going into a particular area of close to $600 million. That money would have to be made up from somewhere else.
If we are looking at a recession period in terms of the economy not being good, I do not think you would need to be any kind of a financial or constitutional or federal-provincial expert to know that a province such as Manitoba would be adversely affected and very seriously affected in the quality possible in health care over the next number of years. Quite certainly a potential is there at least to cause the quality to deteriorate significantly.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
The situation is felt with such intensity in the province of Manitoba that the opposition literally has joined forces in terms of opposing and trying to put forward a positive voice and a positive position to the Minister of Finance. As far as the Manitoba Members of Parliament are concerned, one has to question the strength of the argument, or whether there was an argument at all. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael) and also the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), were trying to convince the minister, the parliamentary secretary and the finance officials, of what will become a growing need over the next number of years for money going into a province such as Manitoba for health and post-secondary education.
I am not going to speak for a great length of time, Mr. Speaker, because like many others in this chamber I am not an expert in this particular area. I know one thing, Mr. Speaker, I know that when you are short of a substantial amount of money, especially in an important area like health care, there will be problems. That is the kind of thing that concerned and disappointed us because the Minister of Finance did not come in with something he could have done, that is, basically, an amendment to allay the fears of particular provinces such as Manitoba.
I do not often quote a provincial minister of Finance. I cannot ever remember quoting a provincial New Democratic Party finance minister in the House of Commons. The minister of finance for the province of Manitoba has, I believe, made some pretty substantial representations to the government in Ottawa. He has put the point forward in a very responsive and straightforward manner when he commented on the whole question of the five-province standard and the so-called representative average standard toward which the government is moving. He made a point-and I think it should be made again here in this House-that it is inconsistent with the equalization principle, which is really soon to become a permanent part of the Constitution. The Constitution resolution is being put into force, I assume, and we will have a chance to take part in the ceremonies a few days from now. The Constitution resolution talks about the whole question of equalization, and says:
Parliament and the Government of Canada are committed to the principle of making equalization payments to ensure that provincial governments have sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of taxation.
That is not going to take place, under this legislation, for some provinces. For example, under Bill C-97 the impact on the provinces between 1982-83 to 1986-87 will be negative, and in the case of Manitoba, it will lose close to $3,000 per family, or $2,786 to be exact. That money has to be made up somewhere, or else the standards will drop. It is as simple as that.
That is the whole essence of the disappointment I feel this afternoon in listening to the Minister of Finance, hoping he would have an amendment or would be more constructive, rather than saying something that most of us in the House have known for a long time. Certainly the government of Manitoba has already included the figures that he put into his statement this afternoon, and have already put into their
projections the shortfall that the government of the province of Manitoba is going to incur. That shortfall will be substantially higher than that of most other provinces. In fact, this $2,700 figure, close to $3,000, that I mentioned earlier, will be five times the average cost for the have provinces and will be 50 per cent higher than the average for the have-not provinces. With 4.2 per cent of the national population and 3.7 per cent of the national output, Manitoba will bear about 10.2 per cent of the net cost of the federal cutbacks. I cannot reinforce enough the fact that this is not fair. The have-not provinces bear about 71.6 per cent of the cutbacks, compared with 43.5 per cent of the population, and 36 per cent of the national output. In contrast, the have provinces bear about 20 per cent of the cutbacks, compared with 50 per cent of the population, and 63 per cent of the national output. It does not make sense. That is not equalization. It is not fair.
Over the next five years, the percentage shares of the equalization payments to Manitoba will plunge by 1.7 per cent. Under the expiring agreement, they would have increased by 1.9 per cent. Obviously those of us who are from the province of Manitoba would like all that we could obtain from the federal government. But surely there must be a happy medium. There must be a meeting area between what members of Parliament representing constituents of Manitoba would like and what the federal government is doing at the present time. The federal government has not found any middle of the road solution in terms of the cost-sharing part of this legislation.
The minister and members of this House know that the very provinces which have little financial room to manoeuvre are receiving the biggest federal cutbacks. That is one of the great problems of Manitoba and of some of the maritime provinces. The economic indicator figures from 1976 to 1981 show Manitoba as the lowest of any province in all three categories of domestic production, employment and investment growth, yet Manitoba is allocated a projected equalization growth rate only slightly more than half the national average. It is 3.27 per cent compared to 6.98 per cent.
Even with those figures, we were not able to convince the federal government to loosen the purse strings and to look at the situation in a more realistic manner. Manitoba simply does not have the resources to absorb a financial blow of this magnitude without the detrimental impact being felt at some time by every resident of Manitoba, whether it is in the north, in Flin Flon, Churchill, The Pas or Thompson, the central part of the province, the southern part, Winnipeg or Brandon. The impact will be felt and will increase over the length of time that this legislation continues to be in effect.
Manitoba just does not have the financial capability to sustain that kind of financial blow which the federal government is trying to impose upon it. Such action by the federal government simply does not make sense. Under the cutbacks, the provinces with the greatest need for development of their
April 5, 1982

economic activity are being rendered the most incapable of generating a particular capability because of what is happening with this bill.
During the five year lifetime of the act, the federal cutback of funds to Manitoba will amount to about $719 million. 1 repeat, the cost will be about $2,800 per family of four. I stress again that this comes at a time of recession, of present and presumably continuing high interest rates, of poor export markets, and at a time when not only Manitoba but all provinces are experiencing a greater number of business bankruptcies than we have seen for a long time.
Manitobans simply cannot afford to pay increased provincial taxes to cover the federal government's shortfall. The money simply is not there. The economic activity is not there.
This situation not only exists in Manitoba but across the country, in some provinces it is to a lesser extent and in others to a greater extent. In the case of the maritime provinces, the situation is more dramatic. These proposals will implement a dramatic decline in real terms of federal support for the basic programs throughout Canada. I do not believe that this act is a product of a substantiated policy.
It appears from discussions with the Minister of Finance, the Manitoba minister of finance and some officials that the policy was not thought out. As I mentioned before, there should be a way for the government and members of the House from Manitoba to find an area between what is proposed in this bill and what is wanted in order to maintain the kind of health and educational standards Manitobans are entitled to. There should be a year in which to make a tradeoff. Obviously that was not to be.
With the federal government pulling back in terms of health care and education, there is the danger of a checkerboard system in this country for health and medical care and education. The possibility exists where the wealthier provinces will benefit. Obviously the western provinces other than Manitoba could have a more sophisticated and up to date health care facility in relation to research, infrastructure and technology than does Manitoba and some of the maritime provinces.
When one looks at the whole program, not only in terms of health care, one wonders why the government went in the direction it did. Virtually every group has been opposed to this part of the bill, including the parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. The Economic Council of Canada did not have much to say that was positive about the method or the direction in which the government is going. The Canadian Council on Social Development, the Business Council on National Issues and most other groups in this country are concerned about the direction in which the government is going. They are concerned about the situation developing-a patchwork situation-with some provinces having better medical components than others.
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Finally, we are disappointed that the Minister of Finance did not see fit to address some problems which are going to be very real in this country for years to come.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-97, an act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977 and to provide for payments to certain provinces.
As you will know from having heard the debate up to the present time, the bill is intended to carry out a number of functions. Its primary purpose is to extend for another five years programs in an act under which major federal-provincial transfer payments are made-specifically the established programs financing plan and the equalization program. The EPF will be amended by terminating its revenue guarantee component and thereby substantially reducing the federal contribution under established programs financing over the next five years.
On the question of equalization, a different formula is being introduced to replace that which has been in place since 1977.
I wish to focus my remarks on the EPF and equalization-related provisions in the context of the Atlantic provinces in general and of my own province of Prince Edward Island in particular. I would like to begin by discussing the established programs financing plan. I have been keenly interested for some time now in this whole issue dealing with arrangements under established programs financing for the financing of postsecondary education, medicare and hospitilization, but my interest was sharpened greatly when the government signalled in its October 28, 1980, budget that it intended to realize substantial net savings in the social development envelope.
Let me quote from that budget, which was a little less infamous, and perhaps a little less offensive, than the recent one. It was stated in the October 1980 budget that:
The government intends to achieve net savings in this area-
That is the social development envelope.
-to help finance initiatives in other envelopes. Because of the statutory nature of much of the spending in this envelope, savings are not assumed to begin until 1982-83. Savings are expected to include reductions in federal transfers to provinces relating to areas coming under provincial jurisdiction. In part, savings may be redeployed within the envelope.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
The reason why I quoted that statement from the budget is that it was the first real signal of the federal government's intentions which have been expressed in the bill we are debating tonight. The cat was partially let out of the bag with the October 28, 1980, budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). If the cat was let out of the bag a little bit in October, 1980, the cat was swiftly kicked out of the bag as a result of a statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) during an interview with the CBC on November 8, 1980, just a few days after the minister brought down his budget. In that interview, the Minister of National Health and Welfare made it clear that the cutbacks to which reference was made in the budget would not be in the health care area. She made it very clear by implication that the federal government's net savings in the social development envelope would be achieved at the expense of the other part of the established programs financing package, namely postsecondary education. The educational system in Canada, especially the post-secondary educational system, is an easy target and a convenient whipping boy for any government which wants to cut expenditures without incurring the wrath of the Canadian public. By its very nature, the Canadian higher education system has too often been docile. Consequently, the Minister of Finance obviously thought that he could slash federal expenditures in that area, where there would not be enormous organized opposition. Of course, health care was not to be spared. But, the fact is that it was in the education area, according to the minister of health, where the government expected to achieve most of its savings. Unfortunately, people's worst suspicions have been realized in Bill C-97.
Let us look for a moment at the established programs financing provisions in the bill. EPF is a major federal-provincial transfer payments program. It is designed to provide funding from the federal treasury for post-secondary education, hospitalization and medicare. The existing EPF arrangements, which are now coming to an end, were set in place in April of 1977. Annual block payments were made to each of the provinces from the federal treasury. Half were in the form of tax transfers; there were various arrangements between the federal government and the provinces in taxation, whereby the federal government created a little room for the provinces to raise money for EPF purposes. The other half under EPF was in the form of cash. Under the 1977 program, which has continued to the present, no conditions were attached to the money intended for post-secondary education. About a third of the government's EPF money was earmarked for post-secondary education. There was, however, no obligation on the part of the provinces to spend the money for post-secondary education, once it was received by the provinces from the federal government. In other words, there was merely an understanding that it would be spent on education.
I have no doubt that the federal government-and to this extent I will give it its due-is right when it argues that the total federal share of the cost of post-secondary education in Canada has increased markedly since 1977. For example, in 1977-78, the federal share was 65 per cent of total provincial expenditures for universities. In 1980-81, this figure had
increased to 76 per cent. The federal government may well have a case-I suspect it does-for saying it is paying a disproportionate share of the total cost of post-secondary education in Canada. The government is probably also right when it argues it is not getting its fair share of the credit for these expenditures. The provinces are doling out the money, having received much of it from the federal treasury. The people, the electorate, see the provinces on the front line and the federal government taking a back seat when it comes to the allocation of political credit. Finally, the federal government is probably right when it argues that it is having too little direct say in how those expenditures are actually made.
However, having conceded those points, I think it is just not good enough to argue on the basis of them that we need a whole new federal-provincial fiscal transfer arrangement of the kind contemplated in Bill C-97. There are legitimate national concerns about post-secondary education. One is that there be maximum accessibility. There is a legitimate national concern about bilingualism. There is a legitimate concern about Canadian studies, manpower planning and research and development. Of course the federal government has a legitimate role to play in the financing of post-secondary education, even though education technically resides within the jurisdiction of the provinces. Such considerations, however, are hardly a justification for the fundamental way in which the government is trying to alter the funding system under Bill C-97.
Of particular concern to me and my colleagues is the planned elimination of the revenue guarantee. The revenue guarantee was a means of compensating the provinces for revenue lost following the 1972 federal tax reforms. Those reforms, after the Carter royal commission reported, would have had the effect of reducing provincial revenues, unless certain compensating provisions were made. So in 1972 the revenue guarantee was instituted, and then in 1977 it became part of the established programs financing parcel. The revenue guarantee was unconditional in the eyes of the provinces. The money was to go into the consolidated revenues of the provinces to support all their programs, and not just higher education, medicare and hospitalization. It was to support all programs right across the board. However, even though that was true, the provinces would never have agreed to the 1977 established programs financing formula in the absence of the revenue guarantee. So the two are very much an integral part of one another. In that sense they are inseparable. But now the federal government, through Bill C-97, is seeking to separate the inseparable. The revenue guarantee is to be abolished. Future contributions by the federal government to or established programs financing are to be calculated without any reference to the revenue guarantee. The result will be a substantial reduction in the total capacity of the provinces to fund health and education.
In this House, and outside the House in forums across the land, the Minister of Finance insists that federal contributions to EPF programs will increase. He has told me, in response to at least five questions on the floor of the House of Commons in
April 5, 1982

the Oral Question Period, that the federal contribution to EPF will increase about 12 per cent per year. He is right if he ignores the revenue guarantee. But, reading between the lines, we find that what he is actually saying is that he will increase funding 12 per cent per year on a much narrower base, the base being shorn of the revenue guarantee, which again was really integral to the established programs financing. The minister is completely ignoring this point. The Minister of Finance is deceiving the Canadian people. I am not saying that is necessarily the result of chicanery. The effect, however, is that the Canadian people are being misled on this important point. There will be a 12 per cent increase per year, or in that neighbourhood, in established programs financing but on a much smaller foundation. The minister's calculations are based strictly on program-directed grants, ignoring totally the sister transfer arrangement, the revenue guarantee. Over the next five years, the federal government will slash EPF by $5.7 billion because of the elimination of the revenue guarantee. In 1982-83, federal savings will be $915 million. That is taking into account the program directed part of established programs financing. When we take into account planned increases for established programs financing per se, together with the elimination of revenue guarantee, the actual cash payments to the provinces under EPF in 1982-83 will be some $400 million less than in 1981-82.
When the budget of November 12 was brought down, the Minister of Finance said that those reductions would be offset partially by increased provincial revenues contemplated by the tax measures in the budget. He predicted a net loss of $1.9 billion over five years. Well, Sir, on November 23, just 11 days after the minister brought his budget down, he had to revise his calculations. He admitted an administrative error of $662 million. I do not know how a government, especially this government, can justify administrative errors of such a magnitude, but that is beside the point. The fact is, the minister conceded there was a $662 million error in his calculations.
Then on December 18 he came into the House and announced at least 20 major transitional changes, as he called them, to his November 12 budget. Some of them, probably most of them, had the effect of restoring benefits to the taxpayer. That restoration in turn had the effect of reducing both federal and provincial revenues originally projected in the budget. So much uncertainty now surrounds the budget, so many changes are being made, and there is such confusion about it, that we still do not know where the provinces will stand once the ways and means motions are presented and voted upon. We do know, though, that the provinces will have a shortfall of at least $5.7 billion because of the elimination of the revenue guarantee.
If I may be allowed to focus on the implication of all this on my own province for a moment, I would point out that the new arrangement means a net loss to Prince Edward Island under established programs financing. In 1981-82 Prince Edward Island received $45 million in EPF, proper, and $3 million under the revenue guarantee part, for a total of $48 million. Under the new system, with the revenue guarantee abolished,
Federal Transfers to Provinces
Prince Edward Island can expect no more than $47 million in 1982-83, $54 million in 1983-84 and $61 million in 1984-85. These projections do not even keep pace with the 12 per cent inflation rate we have had in the country. These amounts will have dire consequences for my tiny province and, indeed, for every province.
At present, the federal government pays in excess of $3 billion for post-secondary education across the country. In 1979-80 $1.6 billion of the total was in cash payments and $1.4 billion in tax points. The $3 billion represents between 65 per cent and 100 per cent of the total spent on post-secondary education in the provinces, from one province to another. In the Atlantic provinces the federal contribution to higher education is about 100 per cent of the total. In my province it is certainly close to that, largely due to a lack of alternative revenue sources.
When the federal government starts to cut back in the area of post-secondary education, the Atlantic provinces are especially vulnerable. In fact, education across Canada will suffer. The provinces, starved of federal funding, will have to squeeze their universities and colleges even harder than they are already squeezed today. Operating grants to post-secondary institutions have grown by only about 41 per cent since 1976, but the consumer price index has jumped 54 per cent in the same period, so the grants are not even keeping up with inflation. Student enrolment has jumped by 70,000 to 630,000 at the university level since 1976. Universities and community colleges are, therefore, being compelled to do much more with much less. The poorer provinces are being hit the hardest.
I need not remind you, Mr. Speaker, that shared-cost programs, almost by definition, are designed to ensure that people across Canada have access to equivalent facilities. The idea is that people are not to be disadvantaged because they lived in Manitoba, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island, say, in terms of receiving some minimal level of services. That principle has now been sacrificed by the government on the high altar of the greed of the Minister of Finance.
Alberta, for example, has all kinds of resource revenue. I do not begrudge them that revenue, but I simply state that the province has the wherewithal to roll with the federal government's punches. As the federal government retrenches in areas such as post-secondary education, Alberta can make adjustments. British Columbia, too, has enormous resources revenue and other wealth. Thus, to some extent it can make adjustments, as can Saskatchewan. Those provinces can adjust as the purse strings are pulled tighter. By contrast, the four Atlantic provinces will be left high and dry to fend for themselves.
The total post-secondary education system in the maritimes costs about $260 million annually to operate, of which $190 million or about 73 per cent is paid by the federal government through transfer arrangements. Of that, $120 million or 46 per cent is in cash transfers. The Atlantic provinces, therefore, are singularly vulnerable to any federal government belt tightening.

April 5, 1982
Federal Transfers to Provinces
I hasten to point out that while we in the Atlantic provinces are particularly disadvantaged in that respect, all provinces are affected. I ask myself what is gained by the efforts of the federal government to lower its deficit at the expense of postsecondary education. What is gained by the federal government's efforts to reduce deficits at the expense of any of the major areas in the social development envelope? All the government is doing is transferring its own deficit to the provinces. That is what 1 call Mickey Mouse economics, Mr. Speaker.
The total public debt is what is important in controlling inflation. It is not important whether the debt is at the federal level, the provincial level or the municipal level. It is the total public debt that fuels and inflames inflation. Transferring public debt from one level of government to the other accomplishes absolutely nothing. It is a cosmetic act. Already, because of the federal and provincial retrenchment of financing for post-secondary education, class sizes have had to be increased, library hours at universities and community colleges have had to be cut, research equipment has become increasingly obsolete and many programs have had to be eliminated or truncated. In Ontario, serious consideration is being given to at least the possibility of closing down four universities and four community colleges. That action may never happen. Yet the very fact that it is being considered reflects the extent of the problem.

speechtext:
Every department, from engineering to liberal arts, is affected; none is insulated. In the process, the quality of education is being allowed to suffer.
One of the things that particularly concerns me is the question of accessibility. Cuts will make it impossible for a large number of children from middle and lower-income families to go to our colleges and universities. Already, a disproportionate number of students from poorer families is exluded from higher education. New funding arrangements given expression in Bill C-97 will make the situation worse. Universities will be forced to increase fees, perhaps massively. There is a direct link between tuition and accessibility, Mr. Speaker. The Stanford Research Institute established that link beyond a shadow of a doubt in 1975. In the Atlantic provinces most families fall in the lower-income category. In Prince Edward Island, the average family income is only about $18,000 per year. If the provinces, because of cutbacks at the federal level, are forced to reduce funding to universities, and if the universities, in turn, are forced to increase tuition fees, the burden will fall most heavily on the poorer people of the country.
I want to conclude on a note about equalization. I am convinced that, however bad the situation is because of established programs financing arrangements being planned, sunshine will not be shed on the situation due to proposed equalization provisions. Since 1967-68, payments have been
based on a national average of fiscal capacity among provinces. Excluded from the calculations was half the revenue from non-renewable resources; excluded as well were all municipal taxes. Any province which fell below a national level so defined was given an equalization payment. The November budget proposed that a substantial change be made in the old formula; payments were to be made on the basis of the Ontario standard. I argued vehemently in the House against the Ontario standard because the Conference Board, for example, had projected that Ontario in the years to come would have the slowest rates of growth of any province. To hitch the wagon of the have-not provinces to Ontario's star would jeopardize, in all likelihood, the sources of revenue of the provinces under equalization.
I welcome the fact that the minister saw the light and abandoned the Ontario standard. Now with a new formula based on a five-provinces average, he has introduced the capacity of five provinces to raise revenue. The new formula includes all revenue from natural resources and municipal taxes. It excludes Alberta and all Atlantic provinces from the five-province average. The new formula provides for a modification, namely, a ceiling and a floor. Both are helpful. I commend the minister for including them. But I believe that the total effect will be potentially disastrous for provinces like my own, and especially Newfoundland and Nova Scotia because as oil and gas revenues in those provinces come on stream their equalization payments will be reduced correspondingly. That provision amounts to virtually a 100 per cent tax on resource revenue. It cannot help but build into the system a disincentive for the have-not provinces to become self-reliant.
At first blush Prince Edward Island stands to gain. We do not have resource revenues or many municipalities. The inclusion of revenue from those sources has the tendency of defining Prince Edward Island as poorer than would otherwise be the case and therefore to strengthen its position in terms of receiving payments under equalization. The statistics also look encouraging. For example, in 1981-82 we will get $103 million; in 1982-83 we will get $124 million; in 1983-84 we will get $140 million. By 1986-87, Prince Edward Island will receive $189 million.
The statistics do not tell the entire story, however. The problem is that Prince Edward Island, the other Atlantic provinces, Manitoba and Quebec have become too dependent upon transfer payments because the government does not realize the value of helping them to become self-reliant. Instead of giving provinces an opportunity to develop their manufacturing sector, they have been weaned on transfer payments. I think the figures bear this out. Total federal transfers to governments, to persons and to businesses in Prince Edward Island will represent 51 per cent of the island's gross domestic product in 1981-82. By contrast, for all Canada total federal transfers will represent only 13 per cent of gross domestic product in the same year. Prince Edward Island receives the highest per capita equalization payments of any
April 5, 1982

province in Canada at the governmental level. In terms of transfer payments to individuals last year, a total of $52.9 million was paid in unemployment insurance benefits, or an average of $426 for every man, woman and child on Prince Edward Island. We have become very dependent on transfer arrangements. However well structured they may be, and no matter what improvements might be introduced, the basic point is that the federal government is relying too much on the transfer approach to economic development at the expense of preventing the Atlantic provinces and region from becoming to a degree self-reliant.
I should like to stress a point which I made in my speech on the Constitution on October 20, 1980. I made the point then- and I stick to it now-that such regional economic servitude is not exclusively the result of neglect or of accident. I went on to say that one cannot overlook the fact that it has served the interests of central Canada to have the Atlantic provinces as a ready market for their manufactured goods, rather than engaged in manufacturing themselves. National policies, from protective tariffs to freight rates, have consistently favoured Ontario and Quebec-the very provinces whose votes have enabled the Liberal Party of Canada to govern the country for most of this century.
I want to conclude by quoting a former premier of Prince Edward Island, Angus MacLean, who said:
Could it be that the central government only responds "in the national interest" when those who are asked to make concessions are minorities in the House of Commons, but never when those expected to make concessions are the numerical majorities? Could it be that, if we had a truly federal state, in which all partners had a more significant voice, national policies might more truly reflect the interests of all provinces and, hence, the entire country?
To my mind Bill C-97, especially with its proposed changes to the established programs financing and equalization arrangements, perpetuates the same faulty approach. That is why I for one oppose the bill, and I wish to do so vigorously.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) is anxiously awaiting my words of wisdom. We always seem to be in the House together when I make a speech condemning the government, quite properly, for its oversights.
Again I stand in the House on another bill as I have done several times before. Bill C-97 has received first reading and second reading in principle when some very major defects were pointed out on all sides of the House, government backbenchers included. Then the bill went into committee stage where amendments were suggested and some very good reasons for them were given. Report stage having been finished, we are at a point where the government has accepted absolutely none of the recommendations or the amendments of my party or of the NDP. It overlooked and blocked, through its caucus process, changes which its own members would have suggested. The government permitted only one amendment which deals with the province of Manitoba. It was so apparent that it was brought to the attention of the government by members on this side and by the provinces. The government had no choice but to go along with it because the unfairness for the people of Manitoba was just too enormous to overlook. The government claims, Mr. Speaker, that the revenue guarantee is the reason it is cutting back. Let me tell you about that revenue guarantee. In 1971, when the then minister of finance, Edgar Benson, brought in tax reform there was great uncertainty as a result of the Carter report. Because of that uncertainty when they signed the agreement in 1971 for fiscal relations applying from 1972 to 1977, the then minister of finance said to the provinces: we will put in this revenue guarantee so that you will not suffer any dramatic negative effects from the new taxation system.
As it turned out, the new system was more harmful to the provinces than the federal government had said it would be, and they had to make a transfer to the provinces under the revenue guarantee. In 1976, with regard to the agreement which would apply from 1977 to 1982, there were discussions about the whole basis of the agreement. The two sides had their respective positions and they simply negotiated until they came up with the 1977 agreement.
During these negotiations the provinces wanted to have four tax points and a certain amount of cash, but the federal government did not agree. They negotiated until the federal government made an offer of $7.60 per capita plus one tax point in lieu of the revenue guarantee. The provinces accepted the offer and the revenue guarantee effectively came to an end. In the yearly transfers from that point on there was no mention at all of the revenue guarantee. Indeed, as further proof of that, Donald Macdonald said in the House that the revenue guarantee had been negotiated away. In addition, the cheques came not from the Department of Finance, as they had from 1972 to 1976, but came in fact from the then minister of national health and welfare for medicare, and the then secretary of state for post-secondary education. That was for the period ending in 1981.
So we then come to a new agreement for 1982-87, and suddenly the federal government says it is going to cut back and is going to take out the revenue guarantee. It skipped back to 1971, ignoring completely the agreement negotiated in 1976, and ignoring the statement by Donald Macdonald that the revenue guarantee had ceased to exist. Why is it we in this country are incapable of learning from the experience of others?
We need to know where we were in the past. We ha\4 to know what the unique role of doctors was. They were selfgoverning. They were self-employed in the sense that they provided their own offices and staff. They worked long, hard hours. I do not think anyone would object to that. know many doctors who earn less than members of the House. Out of that lesser income, they must provide their office, staff and their own pension. That is what I am saying. Why not be honest with the doctors? If Canadians want doctors to be civil servants, why do we not enter into that negotiation? Here is what we would have to do.
We would have to say to the doctor that he will have this type of salary. Let us assume it is the same as we receive. Members of the NDP are often critical of doctors, but they sure take their $65,000, some $16,300 of which is tax free. We could turn to the doctors and say that we will give them $75,000, which will put them on a par with Members of Parliament. They could have access to the same type of pension, 5 per cent a year. After six years, each member of the NDP will either resign from the House or be thrown out and collect a pension of a minimum of 30 per cent.

I am condemning the hypocrisy of the NDP. I have a feeling that if we went to the doctors and offered them $75,000 a year with the same pension plan as that of Members of Parliament, deputy ministers and senior management, and provided them with office space and staff that Members of Parliament and others receive, and required them to work 37.5 hours a week as do civil servants, every doctor in the land would accept that. If they could get in the trough with that kind of money, they would be in it. Why do we not do that? The cost to the Canadian people would be billions of dollars.
I want to deal with the incomes of doctors. The NDP talk about $100,000. That is not correct. It is true that some specialists make a lot of money, but the average GP works 60 to 70 hours a week. That is why his income is as high as it is. He puts in super-long hours. If a doctor worked 37.5 hours a week, he would earn only half as much as a Member of Parliament. If the Canadian people had to choose between their doctor or their Member of Parliament, they would choose their doctor. When I travelled across the country, including my travels with the task force, I gained a very strong feeling that people favour their doctors. They appreciate the hard work their doctors do. For the NDP to challenge that is just incredible.
The hon. member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill went after the doctors today. He challenged them. If he is going to criticize them and then portray doctors to us as being good people, why does he not say one good word about them? I have never heard that hon. member say anything good about doctors.
Post-secondary education is another critical issue in our society. The cutbacks here are going to hurt more than anywhere else. By making these cutbacks in the Atlantic provinces, the Liberals are attacking the future of the nation. Just
as the deficit places a burden on future generations, cutting back support for post-secondary education will also affect the future. There will be fewer people coming out of our universities and colleges who are adequately trained to take on the challenges of the future. That is bad.
Today the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) made a funny statement about EPF. He said the universities were not meeting the national goals, not responding to the imperatives of the federal government. When I asked him to clarify that, he did not do very well. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) made an interesting comment with regard to the reason for the cutbacks. He said the federal government is going to determine where the money goes because his own province of Quebec uses the money for ulterior purposes.
That may well be, because that province has an elected separatist government that is doing some mighty funny things. However, let us not make cutbacks in all the other provinces, because of a separatist government in Quebec. For years and years people have had to move out of the Atlantic provinces in order to find jobs. The taxpayers in the Atlantic provinces have been keeping the institutions going, providing some of the top graduates in every discipline, but these graduates have had to go to other parts of Canada to find work. So it is quite appropriate that the federal government should transfer enormous amounts of money for education. Maybe it should be 100 per cent.
